arteries: Descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery
Descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery
Mylohyoid branch of inferior alveolar artery
Frontal branch of superficial temporal artery
Mental branch of inferior alveolar artery
Mental branch of inferior alveolar artery
Mental branch of inferior alveolar artery

Axillary nerve.course: Leaves the axilla through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery and winds around the surgical neck of the humerus.
Axillary nerve.sensory: Skin over the lower deltoid (regimental badge area), via the superior lateral brachial cutaneous nerve.
Axillary nerve.clinical: Injured in fractures of the surgical neck of the humerus and shoulder dislocations: weak abduction and numbness over the lower deltoid.
muscles: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle

Radial nerve.course: Runs with the deep brachial artery in the radial groove of the humerus, then in front of the lateral epicondyle, where it divides into superficial and deep branches.
Radial nerve.sensory: Back of the arm, forearm and the lateral dorsum of the hand.
Radial nerve.clinical: Injured in mid-shaft fractures of the humerus: wrist drop (loss of wrist and finger extension).

Deep branch of radial nerve.course: Pierces supinator and continues as the posterior interosseous nerve.
Deep branch of radial nerve.clinical: Can be compressed where it enters supinator (arcade of Frohse): weak finger extension without sensory loss.

Superficial branch of radial nerve.sensory: Lateral dorsum of the hand and the dorsum of the lateral three and a half digits as far as the distal phalanges.
Superficial branch of radial nerve.course: Runs under brachioradialis, then crosses the anatomical snuffbox.

Posterior interosseous nerve of forearm.course: Runs between the superficial and deep extensor muscles on the interosseous membrane.
Posterior interosseous nerve of forearm.clinical: Injury causes finger drop with preserved wrist extension (extensor carpi radialis longus is spared).
muscles: Humeral head of extensor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris

Musculocutaneous nerve.course: Pierces coracobrachialis and runs between biceps and brachialis, ending as the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve.
Musculocutaneous nerve.sensory: Lateral forearm (via the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve).

Median nerve.from: Lateral and medial cords of brachial plexus
Median nerve.course: Runs with the brachial artery in the arm, through the cubital fossa and between the heads of pronator teres, then through the carpal tunnel.
Median nerve.sensory: Lateral palm and the palmar surface of the lateral three and a half digits.
Median nerve.clinical: Compressed in the carpal tunnel (carpal tunnel syndrome): numbness of the lateral fingers and thenar wasting.
branches: Common palmar digital branches of median nerve
muscles: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis

Anterior interosseous nerve of forearm.course: Runs on the interosseous membrane with the anterior interosseous artery.
Anterior interosseous nerve of forearm.clinical: Injury prevents the thumb–index 'OK' sign (weak flexor pollicis longus and the lateral flexor digitorum profundus) without sensory loss.

Ulnar nerve.course: Passes behind the medial epicondyle (the 'funny bone'), enters the forearm between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris and reaches the hand through Guyon's canal.
Ulnar nerve.sensory: Medial hand and the medial one and a half digits.
Ulnar nerve.clinical: Injured at the elbow or wrist: claw hand of the ring and little fingers, weak finger abduction and adduction.
muscles: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris

Deep branch of ulnar nerve.course: Passes between abductor and flexor digiti minimi and follows the deep palmar arch across the palm.
muscles: Deep head of flexor pollicis brevis
Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand

Dorsal scapular nerve.course: Pierces scalenus medius and runs along the medial border of the scapula.

Long thoracic nerve.course: Descends on the outer surface of serratus anterior in the medial wall of the axilla.
Long thoracic nerve.clinical: Injury (e.g. in axillary surgery) paralyses serratus anterior: winged scapula.

Suprascapular nerve.course: Passes through the suprascapular notch below the superior transverse scapular ligament.
Suprascapular nerve.clinical: Can be entrapped at the suprascapular or spinoglenoid notch: weak shoulder abduction and lateral rotation.

Subclavian nerve.course: Small nerve to subclavius; may contribute an accessory root to the phrenic nerve.

Lateral pectoral nerve.course: Pierces the clavipectoral fascia to reach pectoralis major.
muscles: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle
Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

Medial pectoral nerve.course: Pierces pectoralis minor to reach pectoralis major.
muscles: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

Thoracodorsal nerve.course: Runs with the thoracodorsal artery on the posterior axillary wall to latissimus dorsi.
Thoracodorsal nerve.clinical: Preserved in breast reconstruction with a latissimus dorsi flap.

Iliohypogastric nerve.sensory: Skin over the iliac crest and above the pubis.

Ilio-inguinal nerve.sensory: Upper medial thigh and the anterior scrotum or labium majus.
Ilio-inguinal nerve.clinical: At risk in inguinal hernia repair.

Genitofemoral nerve.course: Emerges on the anterior surface of psoas major.
Genitofemoral nerve.sensory: Small area of the upper anterior thigh (femoral branch) and the scrotum or labium (genital branch).
Genitofemoral nerve.clinical: Its genital branch supplies cremaster and is the efferent limb of the cremasteric reflex (the afferent limb is its femoral branch and the ilio-inguinal nerve).

Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.course: Passes under or through the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine.
Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.clinical: Compression near the ASIS causes meralgia paraesthetica (burning numbness of the lateral thigh).

Femoral nerve.course: Runs in the groove between psoas and iliacus and enters the thigh under the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral artery (outside the femoral sheath).
Femoral nerve.sensory: Anterior thigh and, via the saphenous nerve, the medial leg and foot.
Femoral nerve.clinical: Injury weakens knee extension and abolishes the knee-jerk reflex.
branches: Anterior cutaneous branches of femoral nerve

Saphenous nerve.course: Runs through the adductor canal, then with the great saphenous vein down the medial leg.
Saphenous nerve.clinical: At risk when the great saphenous vein is harvested or stripped.
branches: Medial crural cutaneous branches of saphenous nerve

Obturator nerve.course: Runs along the lateral pelvic wall and leaves through the obturator canal, dividing into anterior and posterior branches around adductor brevis.
Obturator nerve.sensory: Small area of the medial thigh.

Sciatic nerve.course: Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis and descends in the posterior thigh, dividing into the tibial and common fibular nerves, usually above the popliteal fossa.
Sciatic nerve.clinical: Avoided by giving gluteal injections in the upper lateral quadrant; compression causes sciatica-like pain down the back of the leg.

Tibial nerve.course: Runs through the popliteal fossa, deep to the calf muscles and behind the medial malleolus through the tarsal tunnel, dividing into the medial and lateral plantar nerves.
Tibial nerve.sensory: Sole of the foot (via the plantar nerves) and the heel.
Tibial nerve.clinical: Compression in the tarsal tunnel causes burning pain in the sole.

Common fibular nerve.course: Follows biceps femoris and winds superficially around the neck of the fibula, where it divides into superficial and deep branches.
Common fibular nerve.sensory: Lateral leg (via the lateral sural cutaneous nerve).
Common fibular nerve.clinical: The most commonly injured nerve of the lower limb, at the neck of the fibula: foot drop and a high-stepping gait.
branches: Sural communicating branch of common fibular nerve

Deep fibular nerve.course: Runs with the anterior tibial artery in the anterior compartment of the leg onto the dorsum of the foot.
Deep fibular nerve.sensory: The web space between the first and second toes.
Deep fibular nerve.clinical: Injury causes foot drop with numbness limited to the first web space.
branches: Muscular branches of deep fibular nerve
Dorsal digital branches of deep fibular nerve

Superficial fibular nerve.course: Runs in the lateral compartment and pierces the deep fascia in the lower leg.
Superficial fibular nerve.sensory: Lower lateral leg and most of the dorsum of the foot.
branches: Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve

Sural nerve.from: Tibial and common fibular nerves (medial sural cutaneous nerve and sural communicating branch)
Sural nerve.course: Runs with the small saphenous vein behind the lateral malleolus.
Sural nerve.sensory: Lateral border of the foot and the lower posterolateral leg.
Sural nerve.clinical: Commonly taken for nerve biopsy and nerve grafts.

Medial plantar nerve.sensory: Medial sole and the plantar surface of the medial three and a half toes (comparable to the median nerve in the hand).
branches: Common plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
muscles: Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis
Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis

Lateral plantar nerve.sensory: Lateral sole and the lateral one and a half toes (comparable to the ulnar nerve in the hand).
branches: Common plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve

Superior gluteal nerve.course: Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis, with the superior gluteal vessels.
Superior gluteal nerve.clinical: Injury weakens the hip abductors: the pelvis drops on the opposite side when standing on the affected leg (positive Trendelenburg sign).

Pudendal nerve.course: Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, hooks around the sacrospinous ligament and enters the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen in the pudendal canal.
Pudendal nerve.sensory: Most of the perineum and the external genitalia.
Pudendal nerve.clinical: Blocked near the ischial spine for pain relief in childbirth (pudendal nerve block).

Posterior femoral cutaneous nerve.sensory: Back of the thigh and popliteal fossa, and part of the perineum.

Intercostal nerves.course: Run in the costal groove of each rib below the posterior intercostal vein and artery (vein–artery–nerve, top to bottom), between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles; T7–T11 continue into the abdominal wall as thoraco-abdominal nerves.
Intercostal nerves.sensory: Chest and abdominal wall in bands (dermatomes): T4 at the nipple, T10 at the umbilicus.
Intercostal nerves.clinical: Chest drains and intercostal blocks are placed just above a rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.

Olfactory nerve (I).course: Bundles of olfactory fibres pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid to the olfactory bulb.
Olfactory nerve (I).clinical: Fractures of the cribriform plate can cause loss of smell (anosmia) and leakage of cerebrospinal fluid from the nose.

Optic nerve (II).course: Runs from the eyeball through the optic canal to the optic chiasma, where fibres from the nasal halves of the retinae cross.
Optic nerve (II).clinical: A lesion of the chiasma (e.g. pituitary tumour) causes loss of both temporal visual fields (bitemporal hemianopia).

Oculomotor nerve (III).course: Leaves the midbrain between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries, runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus and enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
Oculomotor nerve (III).clinical: Compression (e.g. by an aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery) causes a 'down and out' eye, drooping eyelid and a dilated pupil (parasympathetic fibres to the sphincter pupillae).

Trochlear nerve (IV).course: The only cranial nerve to leave the back of the brainstem; long, thin course around the midbrain and through the cavernous sinus to the superior orbital fissure.
Trochlear nerve (IV).clinical: Injury causes vertical double vision, worse when looking down (e.g. going downstairs).

Trigeminal nerve (V).course: Large sensory root and small motor root leave the pons; the trigeminal ganglion gives rise to the ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2) and mandibular (V3) nerves.
Trigeminal nerve (V).sensory: Face, scalp to the vertex, cornea, nasal and oral cavities, teeth.
Trigeminal nerve (V).clinical: Trigeminal neuralgia: brief, severe shooting pain in one of its divisions. The corneal reflex tests its ophthalmic division.

Ophthalmic nerve.course: Runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus and enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
Ophthalmic nerve.sensory: Forehead, upper eyelid, cornea and the bridge of the nose.
Ophthalmic nerve.clinical: Shingles of this division (herpes zoster ophthalmicus) can involve the eye.

Maxillary nerve.course: Leaves the skull through the foramen rotundum into the pterygopalatine fossa and continues as the infra-orbital nerve.
Maxillary nerve.sensory: Cheek, lower eyelid, upper lip, upper teeth, palate and the nasal cavity.

Inferior alveolar nerve.course: Enters the mandibular foramen and runs in the mandibular canal, giving the mental nerve at the mental foramen.
Inferior alveolar nerve.sensory: Lower teeth, and the chin and lower lip via the mental nerve.
Inferior alveolar nerve.clinical: Anaesthetised near the mandibular foramen for lower dental work (inferior alveolar nerve block).

Lingual nerve.course: Joined by the chorda tympani (facial nerve), it runs beside the third molar into the floor of the mouth.
Lingual nerve.sensory: General sensation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (taste via the chorda tympani).
Lingual nerve.clinical: At risk in removal of lower wisdom teeth.

Mental nerve.course: Emerges from the mental foramen below the second premolar.
Mental nerve.sensory: Skin of the chin and the lower lip.

Buccal nerve.sensory: Skin and mucosa of the cheek (it is sensory; buccinator is supplied by the facial nerve).

Facial nerve (VII).course: Leaves the brainstem at the pontocerebellar angle, runs through the internal acoustic meatus and the facial canal of the temporal bone, exits through the stylomastoid foramen and divides in the parotid gland into temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches.
Facial nerve (VII).sensory: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (chorda tympani); it also carries secretomotor fibres to the lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands.
Facial nerve (VII).clinical: Bell's palsy: sudden weakness of one whole side of the face. A central (upper motor neuron) lesion spares the forehead.

Vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII).course: Runs with the facial nerve through the internal acoustic meatus to the inner ear.
Vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII).clinical: A vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) causes one-sided hearing loss and tinnitus.

Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX).course: Leaves the skull through the jugular foramen and passes between the internal and external carotid arteries.
Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX).sensory: Taste and general sensation from the posterior third of the tongue, the pharynx (afferent limb of the gag reflex), the carotid sinus and body; parasympathetic fibres to the parotid gland.

Vagus nerve (X).course: Leaves the skull through the jugular foramen, descends in the carotid sheath and through the thorax to the abdomen. The right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the subclavian artery, the left under the arch of the aorta.
Vagus nerve (X).sensory: Larynx, pharynx, thoracic and abdominal viscera; parasympathetic supply of the heart, lungs and gut as far as the left colic flexure.
Vagus nerve (X).clinical: Injury to a recurrent laryngeal nerve (e.g. in thyroid surgery) causes hoarseness; the uvula deviates away from the side of a vagus lesion.
muscles: Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid muscle

Accessory nerve (XI).course: Spinal root from upper cervical segments ascends through the foramen magnum and leaves through the jugular foramen; crosses the posterior triangle of the neck superficially.
Accessory nerve (XI).clinical: Easily injured in the posterior triangle (e.g. lymph node biopsy): drooping shoulder and weak shoulder shrug.

Hypoglossal nerve (XII).course: Leaves the skull through the hypoglossal canal, loops forward below the posterior belly of digastric and above the hyoid into the tongue.
Hypoglossal nerve (XII).clinical: On protrusion, the tongue deviates towards the side of the injured nerve.

Abducens nerve (VI).course: Long intracranial course over the petrous apex and through the cavernous sinus beside the internal carotid artery.
Abducens nerve (VI).clinical: Often affected by raised intracranial pressure: the eye cannot move outward and horizontal double vision results.

muscles: Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

Ascending aorta.supplies: The heart, through the coronary arteries arising from its sinuses.

Aortic arch.clinical: Lies behind the manubrium at the level of the sternal angle (T4–T5).

Thoracic aorta.supplies: Thoracic wall, oesophagus, bronchi and pericardium.
Thoracic aorta.clinical: Passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at T12 to become the abdominal aorta.

Abdominal aorta.supplies: Abdominal organs, the posterior abdominal wall and, via the iliac arteries, the pelvis and lower limbs.
Abdominal aorta.clinical: Divides into the common iliac arteries at L4 (level of the iliac crests). Abdominal aortic aneurysms usually form below the renal arteries.

Brachiocephalic trunk.supplies: Right side of the head and neck and the right upper limb.

Right common carotid artery.clinical: Its pulse is felt at the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid; it bifurcates at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C3–C4).

Left common carotid artery.clinical: Bifurcates at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C3–C4).

Internal carotid artery.supplies: Most of the cerebral hemisphere and the eye; it gives no branches in the neck.
Internal carotid artery.clinical: Atherosclerosis at its origin is a common source of stroke and transient loss of vision.

External carotid artery.supplies: The neck, face, scalp and jaws.

Facial artery.supplies: The face, tonsil and submandibular gland.
Facial artery.clinical: Its pulse is felt where it crosses the lower border of the mandible at the front of masseter.

Maxillary artery.supplies: Jaws, teeth, muscles of mastication, palate, nasal cavity and dura mater.
muscles: Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

Middle meningeal artery.supplies: The dura mater and the inner surface of the skull.
Middle meningeal artery.clinical: Enters the skull through the foramen spinosum; tearing under the pterion causes an extradural haematoma.

branches: Frontal branch of superficial temporal artery
Superficial temporal artery.clinical: Its pulse is felt in front of the ear; it is biopsied in suspected giant-cell arteritis.

Occipital artery.supplies: The back of the scalp and upper neck muscles.

Ophthalmic artery.supplies: The eye, orbit and parts of the forehead and nose.
Ophthalmic artery.clinical: Blockage of its central retinal branch causes sudden painless loss of vision.

Vertebral artery.supplies: Spinal cord, brainstem, cerebellum and (via the basilar artery) the occipital lobes.
Vertebral artery.clinical: Ascends through the transverse foramina of C6–C1 and enters the skull through the foramen magnum; the two unite to form the basilar artery.

branches: Medial pontine branches of basilar artery
Lateral pontine branches of basilar artery
Basilar artery.supplies: Brainstem, cerebellum and the back of the cerebrum.

Anterior cerebral artery.supplies: Medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes.
Anterior cerebral artery.clinical: A stroke in its territory weakens the opposite leg more than the arm.

branches: Insular branches of middle cerebral artery (M2)
Middle cerebral artery (M1-segment).supplies: Most of the lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere and, via its striate branches, the internal capsule and basal ganglia.
Middle cerebral artery (M1-segment).clinical: The most common site of stroke: weakness and numbness of the opposite face and arm, and language problems when the dominant hemisphere is affected.

Posterior cerebral artery.supplies: Occipital lobe and the inferior temporal lobe.
Posterior cerebral artery.clinical: A stroke in its territory causes loss of the opposite half of the visual field.

Right subclavian artery.clinical: Becomes the axillary artery at the outer border of the first rib.

Left subclavian artery.clinical: Becomes the axillary artery at the outer border of the first rib.

Thyrocervical trunk.supplies: Thyroid gland, larynx, neck muscles and the scapular region.

Internal thoracic artery.supplies: The anterior chest wall, breast and diaphragm.
Internal thoracic artery.clinical: Runs about 1 cm lateral to the sternum; commonly used as a coronary bypass graft.
muscles: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle
Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

Axillary artery.supplies: Shoulder, axilla and lateral chest wall.
Axillary artery.clinical: Divided into three parts by pectoralis minor; becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major.

Subscapular artery.supplies: Subscapularis, the posterior scapular muscles and latissimus dorsi; it forms part of the scapular anastomosis.

Brachial artery.supplies: The arm and, through its terminal branches, the forearm and hand.
Brachial artery.clinical: Its pulse is felt medial to the biceps tendon at the elbow; it is where blood pressure is measured.

Deep brachial artery.supplies: Triceps and the back of the arm.
Deep brachial artery.clinical: Runs with the radial nerve in the radial groove of the humerus.
muscles: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle

branches: Palmar carpal branch of radial artery
Radial artery.clinical: Its pulse is felt at the wrist lateral to flexor carpi radialis; used for arterial blood gases and coronary catheterisation.
muscles: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis
Deep head of flexor pollicis brevis

branches: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery
muscles: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand

Common interosseous artery.supplies: Deep muscles of the forearm, through the anterior and posterior interosseous arteries.

Superficial palmar arch.from: Ulnar artery (completed by the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery)
Superficial palmar arch.clinical: Lies at the level of the distal border of the outstretched thumb (Kaplan's line).
muscles: Superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis

Deep palmar arch.from: Radial artery (completed by the deep branch of the ulnar artery)
Deep palmar arch.clinical: Lies about 1 cm proximal to the superficial arch, on the bases of the metacarpals. The Allen test checks that both arches fill from either artery.
muscles: Deep head of flexor pollicis brevis
Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand

Coeliac trunk.supplies: The foregut: stomach, liver, gallbladder, spleen, part of the pancreas and the first half of the duodenum.
Coeliac trunk.clinical: Arises at T12, just below the aortic hiatus.

Splenic artery.supplies: Spleen, pancreas (body and tail) and part of the stomach.
Splenic artery.clinical: A tortuous artery running along the upper border of the pancreas.

Superior mesenteric artery.supplies: The midgut: from the second half of the duodenum to the distal transverse colon.
Superior mesenteric artery.clinical: Arises at L1; the left renal vein and the third part of the duodenum pass between it and the aorta.

Inferior mesenteric artery.supplies: The hindgut: distal transverse colon to the upper anal canal.

Left renal artery.clinical: Shorter than the right renal artery.

Right renal artery.clinical: Longer than the left; passes behind the inferior vena cava.

Common iliac artery.clinical: Divides in front of the sacro-iliac joint, where the ureter crosses it.

branches: Anterior division of internal iliac artery
Posterior division of internal iliac artery
Internal iliac artery.supplies: Pelvic organs, perineum, gluteal region and medial thigh.

External iliac artery.clinical: Becomes the femoral artery behind the inguinal ligament.

Femoral artery.clinical: Its pulse is felt at the mid-inguinal point; the usual access route for cardiac catheterisation. It becomes the popliteal artery at the adductor hiatus.

Deep femoral artery.supplies: Most of the thigh muscles and the femur.

Medial circumflex femoral artery.supplies: Adductor muscles and, importantly, the head and neck of the femur.
Medial circumflex femoral artery.clinical: Damage in displaced fractures of the femoral neck can cause avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

Popliteal artery.clinical: The deepest structure in the popliteal fossa; its pulse is felt with the knee flexed. Can be torn in knee dislocations.

Dorsalis pedis artery.clinical: Its pulse is felt lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus.

branches: Calcaneal branches of posterior tibial artery
Posterior tibial artery.supplies: Posterior compartment of the leg and the sole.
Posterior tibial artery.clinical: Its pulse is felt behind the medial malleolus.

Fibular artery.supplies: Lateral compartment muscles and the fibula.

Plantar arch.from: Lateral plantar artery (completed by the deep plantar artery)

Pulmonary trunk.supplies: Carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
Pulmonary trunk.clinical: Divides in the concavity of the aortic arch at the level of T4–T5.

branches: Right inferolateral branch of right coronary artery
Right coronary artery.supplies: Right atrium and ventricle, and in most people the sinu-atrial and atrioventricular nodes and the inferior wall of the left ventricle.
Right coronary artery.clinical: Occlusion causes an inferior myocardial infarction and may disturb the heart rhythm.

Left coronary artery.supplies: Most of the left ventricle, the left atrium and the anterior interventricular septum.

branches: Septal branches of anterior interventricular artery
Anterior interventricular artery.supplies: Anterior walls of both ventricles and the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum.
Anterior interventricular artery.clinical: The most frequently blocked coronary artery (the 'widow-maker' when occluded near its origin).

Superior vena cava.drains: Head, neck, upper limbs and chest wall (via the brachiocephalic and azygos veins).
Superior vena cava.clinical: Compression by a tumour (superior vena cava syndrome) causes swelling of the face and arms.

Inferior vena cava (abdominal part).clinical: Formed at L5 by the union of the common iliac veins, to the right of the aorta.

Inferior vena cava (thoracic part).clinical: Passes through the caval opening of the diaphragm at T8.

Hepatic portal vein.drains: Gastrointestinal tract, spleen and pancreas, carrying absorbed nutrients to the liver.
Hepatic portal vein.clinical: Formed behind the neck of the pancreas. Raised pressure (portal hypertension, e.g. in cirrhosis) opens portosystemic shunts such as oesophageal varices.

Internal jugular vein.clinical: Runs in the carotid sheath lateral to the common carotid artery; a common site for central venous catheters.

External jugular vein.clinical: Visible crossing sternocleidomastoid; distended when venous pressure is raised.

Azygos vein.clinical: Arches over the root of the right lung; an important collateral route if the venae cavae are blocked.

Great saphenous vein.drains: Superficial tissues of the medial leg and thigh.
Great saphenous vein.clinical: Passes in front of the medial malleolus; the longest vein in the body, used for coronary bypass grafts and prone to varicosities.

Small saphenous vein.drains: Lateral foot and back of the leg.
Small saphenous vein.clinical: Passes behind the lateral malleolus with the sural nerve.

Cephalic vein.drains: Lateral (radial) side of the upper limb.
Cephalic vein.clinical: Runs in the deltopectoral groove; often used for pacemaker leads.

Basilic vein.drains: Medial (ulnar) side of the upper limb.
Basilic vein.clinical: Joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein; used for PICC lines.

Median cubital vein.drains: Connects the cephalic and basilic veins in front of the elbow.
Median cubital vein.clinical: The usual site for drawing blood.

Femoral vein.clinical: Medial to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle; deep vein thrombosis often involves it.

Coronary sinus.drains: Most of the heart wall (great, middle and small cardiac veins).
Coronary sinus.clinical: Runs in the posterior coronary groove; used in cardiac resynchronisation (pacing leads).

muscles: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle
Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle
Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle
Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle
Dorsal parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles
Ventral parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles
Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Humeral head of extensor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Humeral head of extensor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris
Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis
Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis
Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis
Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis
Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid muscle

Clavicle.features: The first bone to ossify; connects the upper limb to the trunk and acts as a strut keeping the shoulder away from the chest.
Clavicle.clinical: The most frequently fractured bone, usually at the junction of its middle and lateral thirds after a fall on an outstretched hand.

Scapula.features: Spine, acromion, coracoid process and glenoid cavity; attachment for 17 muscles.
Scapula.clinical: Winging of the scapula indicates serratus anterior or long thoracic nerve weakness.

Humerus.features: Head, anatomical and surgical necks, greater and lesser tubercles, deltoid tuberosity, radial groove, capitulum and trochlea, medial and lateral epicondyles.
Humerus.clinical: Nerves at risk in fractures: axillary (surgical neck), radial (mid-shaft) and ulnar (medial epicondyle).

Radius.features: Head, neck, radial tuberosity and styloid process; lateral bone of the forearm, it rotates around the ulna in pronation and supination.
Radius.clinical: The distal radius is the most commonly fractured site in adults (e.g. Colles fracture after a fall on an outstretched hand).

Ulna.features: Olecranon, coronoid process, trochlear notch, radial notch, head and styloid process; medial bone of the forearm.

Scaphoid bone.features: The largest bone of the proximal carpal row, felt in the anatomical snuffbox.
Scaphoid bone.clinical: The most commonly fractured carpal bone; blood enters mainly at its distal end, so fractures of its waist can lead to avascular necrosis of the proximal part.

Lunate bone.clinical: The most commonly dislocated carpal bone; a dislocated lunate can compress the median nerve.

Hamate bone.features: Its hook forms the lateral wall of the ulnar canal (Guyon's canal) and part of the carpal tunnel.

Pisiform bone.type: Sesamoid bone (in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris)

Hip bone.features: Formed by the ilium, ischium and pubis, which fuse in the acetabulum at about 16 years.
Hip bone.clinical: The anterior superior iliac spine and iliac crest are key surface landmarks; the iliac crest is a common bone-marrow biopsy site.

Femur.features: The longest and strongest bone: head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters, linea aspera, medial and lateral condyles.
Femur.clinical: Fractures of the femoral neck are common in older people and can damage the blood supply to the head (avascular necrosis).

Patella.features: The largest sesamoid bone; increases the leverage of the quadriceps.
Patella.clinical: Tends to dislocate laterally; the low vastus medialis fibres resist this.

Tibia.features: Weight-bearing bone of the leg: condyles, tibial tuberosity, subcutaneous anterior border and medial surface, medial malleolus.
Tibia.clinical: Its shaft is the most common site of open fractures, as much of it lies just under the skin.

Fibula.features: Slender, mostly non-weight-bearing bone: head, neck and lateral malleolus.
Fibula.clinical: The common fibular nerve winds around its neck and is injured in fractures there (foot drop).

Talus.features: Transmits body weight from the leg to the foot; no muscles attach to it and much of it is covered with cartilage.
Talus.clinical: Fractures of its neck can cause avascular necrosis of its body.

Calcaneus.features: The largest tarsal bone (heel); the calcaneal tendon attaches to its posterior surface; the sustentaculum tali supports the talus.
Calcaneus.clinical: Fractured in falls from a height, often together with the lumbar spine.

Navicular bone.features: Its tuberosity on the medial side of the foot receives the main tendon of tibialis posterior.

Cuboid bone.features: A groove on its plantar surface carries the tendon of fibularis longus.

articulates: Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of foot
Fifth metatarsal bone.clinical: Avulsion of the tuberosity or a Jones fracture of the proximal shaft follows inversion injuries.

articulates: Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand
First metacarpal bone.features: Its saddle-shaped joint with the trapezium gives the thumb its wide range of movement, including opposition.
First metacarpal bone.clinical: Fractures at its base (Bennett fracture) involve the carpometacarpal joint.

articulates: Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of hand
Fifth metacarpal bone.clinical: Fracture of its neck from punching is a 'boxer's fracture'.

Manubrium of sternum.features: Jugular notch on its upper border; joins the body of the sternum at the sternal angle (level of the second costal cartilage and the T4–T5 disc).

Body of sternum.features: Receives the costal cartilages of ribs 2–7.
Body of sternum.clinical: Chest compressions in CPR are applied over its lower half.

Xiphoid process.features: Lies at the level of T10; attachment for the linea alba and the diaphragm.

First rib.features: The shortest, broadest and most curved rib; its upper surface is grooved by the subclavian artery and vein, separated by the scalene tubercle (scalenus anterior).
First rib.clinical: Pressure on structures crossing it causes thoracic outlet syndrome.

Twelfth rib.features: Has no anterior attachment; attachment for quadratus lumborum and the diaphragm.

Atlas (C1).features: A ring with no body or spinous process; its lateral masses carry the skull (atlanto-occipital joints: the 'yes' movement).

Axis (C2).features: Its dens projects up into the atlas and acts as the pivot of the atlanto-axial joints (the 'no' movement).
Axis (C2).clinical: Fractures of the dens and of the pedicles (hangman's fracture) can injure the spinal cord.

Vertebra C7.features: Vertebra prominens: its long spinous process is the first easily felt at the base of the neck.

Vertebra L4.features: A line joining the highest points of the iliac crests (supracristal plane) crosses the L4 spinous process or L4–L5 interspace.
Vertebra L4.clinical: Lumbar puncture is done at L3–L4 or L4–L5, below the end of the spinal cord (L1–L2 in adults).

Sacrum.features: Forms the back of the pelvis; the sacral promontory, four pairs of sacral foramina and the sacral hiatus.
Sacrum.clinical: Caudal epidural anaesthesia is given through the sacral hiatus.

Coccyx.features: Attachment for gluteus maximus, coccygeus and the anococcygeal ligament.

Frontal bone.features: Forms the forehead and the roofs of the orbits; contains the frontal sinuses.

Parietal bone.features: Forms most of the roof and sides of the skull.
Parietal bone.clinical: The pterion, where it meets the frontal, sphenoid and temporal bones, is thin and overlies the middle meningeal artery.

Temporal bone.features: Squamous, petrous, tympanic and mastoid parts; houses the middle and inner ear and the facial canal; forms the temporomandibular joint with the mandible.

Occipital bone.features: Surrounds the foramen magnum; occipital condyles, external occipital protuberance and nuchal lines.

Sphenoid bone.features: Body with the sella turcica (pituitary gland) and sphenoidal sinus, greater and lesser wings, pterygoid processes; pierced by the optic canal, superior orbital fissure, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum.

Ethmoid bone.features: Cribriform plate (olfactory nerves), perpendicular plate of the nasal septum, superior and middle conchae, and the ethmoidal air cells.

Maxilla.features: Upper jaw: carries the upper teeth, forms most of the hard palate, the floor of the orbit and contains the maxillary sinus.
Maxilla.clinical: Fractures of the midface are classified as Le Fort I–III.

Mandible.features: The only movable bone of the skull: body, ramus, angle, coronoid and condylar processes, mental foramen and mandibular foramen.
Mandible.clinical: Often fractured in two places, as it forms a ring with the skull base.

Zygomatic bone.features: The cheekbone; forms the lateral wall and floor of the orbit and part of the zygomatic arch.

Nasal bone.clinical: The most commonly fractured facial bone.

Hyoid bone.features: Lies at C3, suspended by muscles and ligaments without articulating with another bone; attachment for the suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles.

Malleus.features: Attached to the tympanic membrane; tensor tympani inserts on it.

Stapes.features: The smallest bone in the body; its footplate fills the oval window; stapedius damps its movement.
Stapes.clinical: Fixation of the footplate (otosclerosis) causes conductive hearing loss.
